title: Describing people: personality
subtitle: thrifty or stingy? frank or blunt?
summary: Describe intelligence, attitudes to life and attitudes to other people - and see how the same characteristic can sound positive or negative depending on the word you choose.

lesson.heading: Intellectual ability
rows: intelligent, bright, clever, sharp, shrewd, able, gifted, talented, brainy (informal)
stupid, foolish, simple, silly, brainless, daft, dumb, dim, thick
clever in a negative way, using brains to trick or deceive
lesson.note: Brainless, daft, dumb, dim and thick are mainly informal, and they can all be offensive.

left.label: Looking outwards
left.text: Some people expect the best and enjoy attention.
examples: Nia is **optimistic** - she looks on the bright side.
Ben is **extroverted** - he loves being the focus of attention.

right.label: Looking inwards
right.text: Others expect the worst and prefer their own company.
examples: Amal is **pessimistic** - he always expects the worst to happen.
Jake is **introverted** - he prefers to be alone with his thoughts.

lesson.heading: Sensible and sensitive - two different words
lesson.text: A **sensible** person is practical and **down-to-earth**; a **sensitive** person is easily hurt. Note also **tense** (or **wound up**, **stressed out**) and its opposite **relaxed**.

examples.text: Eva is very **sensible** - she'd never do anything stupid.
Roberto is very **sensitive** - he gets very **upset** if he feels people are criticising him.
examples.note: worked-up is a more informal alternative to upset

examples.text: I feel very **tense** after a busy day at work but, after a hot bath, I'll soon feel **relaxed**.

lesson.heading: Attitude towards other people
rows: unhappy if others have what you don't

lesson.heading: One person's meat is another person's poison
lesson.text: Some characteristics can be positive or negative depending on your point of view. The pairs below mean roughly the same thing, but the second word in each pair carries a **negative connotation**.

examples.note: negative - the same behaviour, disapproved of

lesson.heading: Positive and negative versions of the same quality

lesson.text: Before you use a personality adjective, ask yourself whether you want to praise or criticise - *determined* and *pig-headed* describe exactly the same behaviour.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its opposite.
Pair the words that have similar meanings.
*Molly's usually frank.* How would you say this to give a negative impression?
exercises.explanation: Frank, direct and open are positive; blunt, abrupt, brusque and curt are the negative versions.

exercises.prompt: *Grace is quite broad-minded.* How would you say this to give a negative impression?
exercises.explanation: Broad-minded is positive; unprincipled and permissive are the negative versions.

exercises.prompt: *Sam can be aggressive.* How would you say this more kindly?
exercises.explanation: Assertive is the positive version of aggressive and bossy.

exercises.prompt: *I find Marcus self-important.* A speaker who admired him would say Marcus was ___.
exercises.explanation: Self-assured and confident are the positive versions of self-important and arrogant.

exercises.prompt: *Don't you think James is nosy?* A speaker who approved would call him ___.
exercises.explanation: Enquiring is the positive version of inquisitive and nosy. (It is more common in writing than in speech.)

exercises.prompt: *Freya is very original.* A speaker who disapproved would call her ___.
exercises.explanation: Unconventional and original are positive; eccentric, odd, peculiar and weird are negative.

exercises.prompt: Match each questionnaire question with the personality adjective it tests.

pairs.left: If you arrange to meet at 7 pm, do you arrive at 7 pm?
When you have a problem, do you think the worst will happen?
Do you find it easy to tell your boss he or she has treated you badly?
Do you always look out of the window if you hear a car draw up?
Do you often buy your friends presents for no particular reason?
Do you frequently disagree with what other people say?

exercises.prompt: Does each adjective praise or criticise?

exercises.statement: A *sensible* person is one who gets upset easily when people criticise them.
exercises.explanation: That describes a sensitive person. A sensible person is practical and down-to-earth.

exercises.statement: *Crafty* and *cunning* both describe someone who uses their brains to trick or deceive.
exercises.explanation: Cunning, crafty and sly all mean clever in a negative way.

exercises.answer: Roberto is very sensitive - he gets upset if people criticise him.
exercises.explanation: Sensitive people are easily hurt by criticism.
